records.place: Manutuke, by the Te Arai River, Gisborne

wine.name: Millton Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: The Te Arai Vineyard, the home block planted from 1984 on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke, on silt loam a few kilometres from the sea and farmed without irrigation.
wine.making: Organically and biodynamically grown fruit is picked by hand in as many as four passes through the vineyard, some years ending with a pass for grapes touched by botrytis. The wine is fermented and raised partly in stainless steel tanks and partly in large 600 litre French oak casks, the size used for Chenin Blanc in the Loire, chosen so that the wood gives texture rather than the taste of oak.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and quince, with mango in warm years and honey where botrytis has come in; a waxy, textured palate, mouth watering acidity and a softening edge of sweetness on the finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fruity on release; like Chenin Blanc of its weight elsewhere, it can gain honeyed depth over several years in bottle.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a little air helps a young bottle; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The home block beside the Te Arai River at Manutuke, the wine's single source.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.
The Loire grape, here raised partly in large French oak casks.

records.table: Millton Vineyards and Winery was founded at Manutuke in 1984 and certified organic in 1989, and its Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc comes from the home block by the river: lime, green apple and honey, a waxy texture and bright acidity. Pour it with fish.
records.story: The family's roots in Gisborne wine go back to 1969, when the parents of one of the founders planted the Opou Vineyard at Manutuke on their sheep station, among the region's early growers. In 1984 the young couple founded their own winery on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke and took over the running of Opou from her parents the same year. They farmed without synthetic sprays from the start, and in 1989 the estate gained organic certification from BioGro, by the accounts of New Zealand Winegrowers and the local press the first wine producer in the country to do so. Biodynamic farming followed, later certified by Demeter, and the house came to be known abroad as a pioneer of both. Chenin Blanc, rare in New Zealand, became its signature: grown on the riverside home block, where autumn mists off the water can bring botrytis, and raised in large casks of the Loire kind. In 2025, after more than forty vintages, the family announced that it would retire the vineyard and itself rather than sell, so the Te Arai Chenin Blanc stands as the record of one family's work. For a sommelier it is the Chenin that tells Gisborne's story.

others.name: Millton Opou Vineyard Chardonnay
others.note: Chardonnay from the family's older vineyard at Manutuke, first planted in 1969.

others.name: Millton Opou Vineyard Riesling
others.note: Riesling from the same vineyard, made in a style with some sweetness.

traps: Te Arai is the riverside home block planted from 1984; Opou is the older family vineyard, first planted in 1969 by the parents of one of the founders.
Millton is a Gisborne house, not Hawke's Bay or Marlborough: Gisborne lies north of both, on the east coast around Poverty Bay.

cards.back: Organic certification from BioGro, by local accounts the first for a New Zealand wine producer.

A long stay in new oak barriques
A blend with late harvest Riesling
Sweet grape juice added before bottling
questions.exp: The home block lies by the Te Arai River, whose autumn mists can bring botrytis, picked in a last pass; the casks are large and chosen to give texture, not new oak flavour.

questions.q: In which year was Millton Vineyards and Winery founded beside the Te Arai River?
questions.exp: The winery was founded in 1984; 1969 is the planting of the family's Opou Vineyard, and 1989 the year of its organic certification.

records.place: Matawhero, on the Poverty Bay flats, Gisborne

wine.name: Matawhero Gewürztraminer
wine.sites: Estate fruit from the Poverty Bay flats on silt loam over clay; the house's Single Vineyard range draws on sites at Riverpoint, Hexton Hills and Patutahi.
wine.making: Picked while the fruit is cool, often by machine in the early morning, then carried quickly to the winery and pressed, as the house's vintage notes describe. It is made as a fresh, fruit led white in a dry or nearly dry style.
wine.glass: Lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight with a touch of ginger; a dry or nearly dry palate, rounded in texture and held by a steely line of acidity, with a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Made for drinking young, in the first few years after the vintage, while its perfume is at its height.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

label.means: The house's range drawn from named Gisborne vineyard sites rather than a regional blend.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.
The pink skinned aromatic grape of Alsace, spelt on the label with its umlaut.

records.table: Matawhero, on the Poverty Bay flats, made its name in the 1970s with Gewürztraminer, and its Single Vineyard Gewürztraminer carries that on: lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight, dry and rounded with a steely line. Pour it with gently spiced dishes.
records.story: In the 1960s a grower planted a vineyard at Matawhero, on the flats outside Gisborne, to supply grapes to the local winemakers. His son brought the family's own label to life in 1975, when the first wines appeared under the Matawhero name, and within a few years his Gewürztraminer had won national and then international acclaim, and the house became known for wine of its own rather than for grapes sold on. Through the 1970s and 1980s the name Matawhero and the grape Gewürztraminer went together in the minds of the country's wine drinkers, and Gisborne, long the engine of bulk white wine, had a fine aromatic white to show. In 2008 the son sold the winery to a new family, who found the house and vineyard run down, rebuilt and replanted the estate and relaunched the label. In 2017 they released the first Irwin Chardonnay, a wine named in tribute to the father and son who had founded the house. The son died in 2023. In 2025 Matawhero marked fifty years since its first wines. For a sommelier its Gewürztraminer is the link between Gisborne's pioneering years and its later wines.

others.name: Matawhero Irwin Chardonnay
others.note: A barrel fermented Chardonnay of the Mendoza clone, made only in fit years and named for the founding father and son; first released in 2017.

traps: Matawhero is both a place on the flats outside Gisborne and the house named after it; it is not a grape or a style.
The house's first wines date from 1975, but the vineyard itself was planted in the 1960s to supply other winemakers.

cards.front: Matawhero: in which year did the first wines appear under its own label?

cards.front: Which grape made Matawhero's name in the 1970s and 1980s?

wine.name: Vinoptima Ormond Reserve Gewürztraminer
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard on Ngakoroa Road at Ormond, inland from Gisborne, planted to Gewürztraminer alone, its first block in 2000.
wine.making: The estate made Gewürztraminer and nothing else. The Reserve was an off dry wine of full weight and ripe alcohol, its fruit and perfume intense enough to make it seem sweeter than it was, and a late harvest wine was made beside it from the same vineyard.
wine.glass: Lychee, rose water and ginger over honey and orange peel; full bodied and oily, off dry, with a long and heavily perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Built to last longer than most Gewürztraminer; the bottles that remain are older vintages, so taste one before pouring it for a guest.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

label.means: The district inland from Gisborne where the estate's single vineyard lay.
The estate's principal wine, beside its late harvest bottling.

records.table: Vinoptima Estate was founded at Ormond in 2000 to make Gewürztraminer alone, and the Ormond Reserve Gewürztraminer was its one wine: off dry, oily and perfumed with lychee and rose. The estate went into receivership in 2018, so older bottles are all that remain.
records.story: The founder came from the family behind the Nobilo winery at Huapai, north west of Auckland, which made the country's first commercial Gewürztraminer in 1972. Years later, in 2000, he founded Vinoptima Estate at Ormond, inland from Gisborne, to make Gewürztraminer and nothing else, a single variety estate rare anywhere outside Alsace. The first block was harvested in 2003, and the Ormond Reserve, with a late harvest wine beside it, became the estate's calling card: rich, off dry and made to age. A second block was planted in 2007. But the wine sold more slowly than it was made, and a stock of well over a hundred thousand litres of Gewürztraminer built up in the cellar. In 2018 the estate went into receivership, its creditors' claims running to millions, and the vineyard and winery were later sold. Vinoptima no longer makes wine. For a sommelier the Ormond Reserve is a lesson in two things at once: what Gisborne's warm, fertile flats can give Gewürztraminer, and how hard it is to build a house on one grape alone.

others.name: Vinoptima Ormond Late Harvest Gewürztraminer
others.note: The estate's sweeter wine from later picked fruit of the same vineyard.

A replacement of the region would be Bushmere Estate (Chardonnay planted in 1972 by New Zealand Winegrowers' profile, its own label later) or Kirkpatrick Estate at Patutahi; neither was researched beyond one search, and the checker should source either before it stands.

The founder is living and never named; the name Nobilo is told only as the family's winery.

records.place: Ormond to Hexton, north of Gisborne

wine.name: TW Chardonnay
wine.sites: The two founding growers' own vineyards on the narrow strip of about five kilometres from Ormond to Hexton north of Gisborne, known locally as the Golden Slope; fruit is picked by hand.
wine.making: Fermented in barriques of French, American and Hungarian oak with wild yeast. After the first fermentation each barrel goes through malolactic fermentation, which gives the blend its creamy texture; the wine is then fined, stabilised, filtered and bottled, as the house's technical notes describe.
wine.glass: Ripe peach and nectarine with grapefruit, over butterscotch, toasted nuts and vanilla from the barrels; full and creamy, with soft acidity and a long, rounded finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and ready on release; it holds for a few years as the fruit turns nutty, but it is made to be drunk rather than laid down.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The initials of the two founding growers' family names.
Printed on the barrel fermented bottling this record describes, above the unoaked Estate Chardonnay.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.

records.table: TW Wines began in 1998, when two Gisborne growers set out to bottle fruit from their own vineyards, and its Reserve Gisborne Chardonnay is the barrel fermented one: ripe peach, butterscotch and toasted nuts, made creamy by malolactic. Pour it with roast chicken or crayfish.
records.story: Gisborne grew Chardonnay for decades before most of its growers made wine of their own, and much of its fruit went to the large wineries of other regions. Two growers whose vineyards lay on the strip between Ormond and Hexton, a slope the locals call the Golden Slope, had seen wines made from their grapes win prizes for others. In 1997, on a fishing trip to Lake Waikaremoana, they hatched the idea of a label of their own, named simply with the initials of their two families. They aimed at the next vintage, found a consultant winemaker, space in a winery and some new French oak barrels, and made their first wines in 1998. The range grew from there: an unoaked Estate Chardonnay, the barrel fermented Reserve, a Chardonnay and Viognier blend, and red wines of Malbec and Merlot. The house remains small and grower owned, a fair picture of a region where the vineyard comes first. For a sommelier the TW Reserve Chardonnay shows the warm, generous Gisborne style that gave the region its name for Chardonnay.

others.name: TW Makauri Merlot Malbec

records.place: Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, North Island

wine.name: Lindauer Classic Brut Cuvée
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the grapes of Champagne, in a non vintage blend.
wine.sites: Bought in and company grown fruit from the warm east coast regions of Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, blended for the house style rather than drawn from one vineyard.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, with its second fermentation in the bottle, and given a year or more on its lees before disgorging, by the accounts of its importer and a New Zealand merchant. It is a non vintage blend finished brut, a dry style.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and white peach with a little toast and vanilla; a lively mousse, crisp acidity and a clean, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two, while the fruit is fresh; it gains nothing from keeping.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a tulip shaped glass or a flute.

label.means: A dry style of sparkling wine, as the brand itself explains the word.
The brand's core range, beside its Special Reserve wines.
A blend of base wines put together for the house style.

records.table: Lindauer is the sparkling brand Montana launched in 1981, named after the painter Gottfried Lindauer, and Classic Brut Cuvée is its core wine: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, bottle fermented, crisp and lemony. Pour it well chilled.
records.story: The name is a painter's. Gottfried Lindauer (1839 to 1926) was born at Pilsen in Bohemia, sailed for New Zealand in 1874 and settled at Woodville, where he painted the portraits of Māori for which he is known; he died there in 1926. In 1981 Montana Wines launched a sparkling wine under his name, and the brand grew into a familiar bottle at home and abroad. Montana's own fortunes ran through the sales of the wine trade: it passed to Allied Domecq in 2001 and, with Allied, to Pernod Ricard in 2005. In 2010 Pernod Ricard sold Lindauer, with several other New Zealand brands, to a consortium led by Lion Nathan with Indevin, and in the same year renamed Montana itself as Brancott Estate, so the two stories part there. The Classic Brut Cuvée, of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, is the brand's core wine. For a sommelier it is the everyday voice of Gisborne's long role as a source of New Zealand's sparkling base wine.

others.name: Lindauer Special Reserve Brut Cuvée
others.note: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, bottle fermented and aged on its lees for two years, by the brand's account.

others.name: Lindauer Free Brut
others.note: An alcohol free wine of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the same two regions.

traps: Lindauer is a brand, not an estate: it has no single vineyard, and its name is a painter's, not a place.
Lindauer began as Montana's brand but left Pernod Ricard in 2010; Brancott Estate, Montana's later name, is a separate house.

report: Pick in doubt, kept: the brand's own Classic Brut page describes a blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from South Australia, while its Brut Cuvée page and a Falstaff listing (Lindauer Classic Gisborne Hawkes Bay Brut Cuvée) give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay. The record follows the latter two; the integrator should confirm which bottle the label means, and a swap to a Gisborne estate (Bushmere Estate or Kirkpatrick Estate) is offered if the Gisborne link is only history.

The method is in conflict: one search summary of the brand's site says many Lindauer wines are made in tank and the vintage wine is the traditional method exception, while an importer and a New Zealand merchant describe the Brut as bottle fermented with twelve to eighteen months on lees. The record says traditional method by those accounts; the checker should settle it.

The launch of 1981 rests on the brand's own Since 1981 and on Tastingbook; the claim that it was the first commercial traditional method wine of the country and the 1980 harvest of Gisborne and Hawke's Bay base wine rest on Tastingbook alone and are left out.
The sale price of 2010 differs by source and is not given; the brand's owners after 2010 are not followed.
Gottfried Lindauer's dates, Pilsen, 1874 and Woodville rest on Te Ara and Wikipedia.
The closing line on Gisborne's role as the source of sparkling base wine draws on the region record and the brand's current Gisborne and Hawke's Bay sourcing; the checker may soften it.
